Priestly Office (of Christ)
PREES-tlee AW-fiss
n. phrase (Christological / munus triplex)
From Latin officium (duty, function, office) + sacerdos (priest). In Reformed theology, the priestly office is one of three offices (munus triplex) by which Christ fulfills His mediatorial work: as Prophet He reveals God's will; as Priest He offers Himself and intercedes; as King He reigns over all.

Biblical Definition

The priestly office of Christ encompasses two inseparable acts: His once-for-all sacrifice on the cross and His ongoing intercession at the right hand of the Father. The letter to the Hebrews is the primary exposition. Christ is “a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens”—not a Levitical priest offering bulls and goats in an earthly sanctuary, but the eternal Son entering the heavenly holy of holies with His own blood (Heb 4:14). Unlike the Levitical priests who died and were replaced, Christ “always lives to make intercession” and is therefore “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.” (Heb 7:25). He did not appoint Himself to this office; the Father designated Him: “Thou art My Son; today I have begotten Thee,” and separately, “So also Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee.” (Heb 5:5). His sacrifice was not coerced but freely offered—“through the eternal Spirit,” He presented “Himself without blemish to God” (Heb 9:14). The priestly office is permanent. The sacrificial work is finished—“It is finished” (John 19:30)—but the intercessory work continues. Every believer's acceptance before the Father rests on Christ's present advocacy. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (8.8) affirms that Christ's priestly work satisfies divine justice, reconciles those for whom He died, and continually presents His merits before the throne.

Webster 1828 Definition

The office by which Christ fulfilled His role as the appointed and eternal High Priest—offering Himself as the perfect sacrifice for sin and now living to make perpetual intercession for those who come to God through Him.

PRIESTLY OFFICE, n. phrase. The second of Christ's three mediatorial offices (munus triplex). As Priest, Christ performs what no Levitical priest could perform: He is simultaneously the Offerer and the Offering, the High Priest and the Victim.

The priestly work has two phases: (1) sacrifice—the single, perfect, unrepeatable offering of Himself at Golgotha, fully satisfying divine justice for the sins of the elect; (2) intercession—His ongoing presentation of the merits of that sacrifice before the Father on behalf of His people.

The Levitical priesthood was a shadow; Christ is the substance. The repeated animal sacrifices pointed forward to His once-for-all offering; the high priest's annual entry into the holy of holies foreshadowed His permanent access to the heavenly sanctuary.

Hebrews 7:25 grounds the believer's full assurance: Christ's intercession is perpetual and infallible. He never sleeps, never forgets, never is overruled. His is a priesthood that cannot pass away.

Rome's error is to repeat the sacrifice in the Mass (re-presentation of Christ's body and blood). Scripture will not allow it: ‘once for all’ (ephapax) marks the sacrifice as definitively complete (Heb 9:26–28).

Key Scripture

Hebrews 4:14 — "Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Hebrews 9:14 — "How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?"

Hebrews 5:5 — "So also Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee."

Modern Corruption

Rome repeats Christ's sacrifice in the Mass; liberalism dissolves His priestly intercession into a merely exemplary martyrdom; charismatic Word-of-Faith teaching bypasses His mediation by claiming direct divine power. All three suppress His unique, perpetual, once-for-all priesthood.

expand to see more

The Roman Catholic Mass presents the Eucharist as a re-presentation or continuation of Christ's sacrifice—the priest at the altar offering Christ anew (though in an “unbloody” manner) to God. This directly contradicts Hebrews' emphatic vocabulary: “once for all” (ephapax; Heb 9:26, 10:10, 10:14), “a single sacrifice for sins for all time,” and “He sat down at the right hand of God”—a posture of completed work. The Reformers rightly identified this as the central sacerdotal error of the medieval church, and the LBCF (29.2) continues to name it as such.

Liberal Christianity, by rejecting penal substitutionary atonement, empties Christ's death of priestly content. What remains is a martyrdom that inspires but does not propitiate, a death that moves God's people but does not satisfy God's justice. Without a genuine priestly sacrifice, there is no real priestly intercession either—only a Jesus who pointed the way but cannot now advocate before the Father for sinners. The believer's confidence collapses without a living High Priest who “always lives to make intercession.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the OT Levitical and Melchizedekian priesthoods as types, fulfilled and surpassed by Christ as the eternal, perfect High Priest who is both Offerer and Offering.

expand to see more

Hebrew kohen — priest; the appointed mediator who stands between God and the people, offering sacrifice and interceding.

Greek archiereus — high priest; the title Hebrews assigns to Christ throughout, elevating Him above the Aaronic order.

Greek ephapax — once for all; Hebrews' signature word affirming the unrepeatable finality of Christ's sacrifice.

Melchizedek — the mysterious priest-king of Salem (Gen 14; Ps 110:4) whose priesthood was royal, eternal, and not Levitical—the OT type of Christ's perpetual priesthood.

Latin propitiatio — propitiation; the satisfaction of divine wrath through the sacrifice Christ offered, the theological heart of the priestly office.

Usage

"The priestly office is the ground of the believer's confidence: every prayer rises to the Father through the mediation of the Son who “always lives to make intercession.”"

"Christ is not only the Offerer but the Offering—He gave Himself, which means His sacrifice has infinite worth, sufficient for every elect sinner in every generation."

"Rome's Mass and Protestant sacramentalism both err in different ways by implying the priestly work is ongoing in the elements; Scripture teaches the sacrifice is finished and the intercession is personal and perpetual."
